title: Puerto Rico Is Rationing Water. It Could’ve Avoided It by Harvesting Rainwater
gist: Puerto Rico is rationing water for 180,000 northeastern households after its driest July on record, but the binding constraint is distribution: the Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority loses roughly 60 percent of drinking water to leaks before it reaches customers, and ruptures in the 72-inch Superaqueduct triggered the emergency. Experts argue decentralized rooftop rainwater harvesting — standard in the US Virgin Islands and Barbados — could capture 30 billion gallons a year from 1 million households at $500–$5,000 per system, but Puerto Rico offers no incentives and even a 2024 law mandating collection on government buildings goes unenforced.

insights.claim: The Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority loses about 60 percent of the island's drinking water to leaking pipes and failing infrastructure before any of it reaches customers' homes, making non-revenue water — not rainfall — the dominant loss in the system.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
entities: Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority
insights.so_what: A 60 percent loss rate defines an enormous addressable market for leak detection, pipe replacement and metering vendors, and makes federal infrastructure dollars for PR a repair-capex story rather than a new-supply story.
insights.quote: loses about 60 percent of the island’s drinking water before any arrives at customers’ homes due to leaking pipes and failing infrastructure
insights.locator: The Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority

insights.claim: The current water emergency in Puerto Rico was caused in part by a series of ruptures in the 72-inch Superaqueduct pipe, a single main artery servicing major cities on the northern coast — a textbook single-point-of-failure risk in centralized water distribution.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
entities: Puerto Rico Aqueduct and Sewer Authority
insights.so_what: Concentration risk in trunk infrastructure is the argument decentralized-water vendors will use in every Caribbean and island bid; watch for redundancy mandates in post-crisis procurement.
insights.locator: The ongoing emergency was caused, in part, by a series of ruptures

insights.claim: Environmental lawyer Ruth Santiago argues the biggest issue in Puerto Rico is government mismanagement of water rather than a lack of it, since abundant water remains available even amid the climate crisis and drought.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: If scarcity is governance-driven rather than hydrological, the investable fix is operations, storage and metering — not desalination or long-haul supply projects.
insights.quote: Even with the climate crisis and these droughts, we still have abundant water
insights.locator: While the drought is a factor, the biggest issue

insights.claim: Puerto Rico governor Jenniffer González ordered municipal governments to shut off water two days at a time in the northeast, leaving 180,000 households with limited access, while many families had already gone without consistent water for more than 100 days.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Multi-month service failure at this scale is the political trigger for emergency appropriations and off-grid household spending on tanks, pumps and filtration.
insights.locator: For the past week, Puerto Rico governor Jenniffer González

insights.claim: Architect Fernando Abruña estimates Puerto Rico could gather 30 billion gallons of water a year if just 1 million households installed rainwater collection, against total residential use of just over 72 billion gallons a year at 62 gallons per resident per day.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Roughly 40 percent of residential demand covered by decentralized capture sizes a real hardware market — gutters, tanks, pumps, filtration — that scales per household rather than per utility contract.
insights.quote: One of the best unused reservoirs of water in Puerto Rico are the roofs of the houses
insights.locator: Abruña, who is also a fellow with the American Institute of Architects

insights.claim: Rainwater harvesting system costs run $500 to $2,000 for small simple gravity-fed units and up to $5,000 for larger units with electric pumps, plus ongoing maintenance and water-quality monitoring costs, according to Plenitud Puerto Rico.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: A $500–$5,000 unit price with recurring maintenance is a serviceable consumer/NGO price point — cheap enough for subsidy programs and rebate-driven volume, unlike utility-scale capex.

insights.claim: The most resilient rainwater systems are purely gravity-fed — gutters diverting roof runoff into a canister connected to indoor pipes — which means they keep working during the grid outages that accompany Caribbean storms.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Gravity-fed designs beat pump-based ones on resilience metrics in grid-fragile markets, favoring low-tech tank and gutter suppliers over electromechanical solutions.
insights.locator: The most resilient harvesting systems rely on gravity

insights.claim: Larger rainwater harvesting systems can supply water for cooling power plants and other industrial uses, extending the addressable market beyond residential potable substitution into industrial process water.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Industrial process-water capture is a higher-ticket segment than household barrels and is where commercial water-tech margins live.
insights.locator: Bigger systems can help collect water

insights.claim: Household rainwater systems in Puerto Rico typically do not provide drinking water, serving non-potable needs like toilet flushing and pet water, which limits their substitution value against utility supply.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Non-potable-only output caps willingness to pay unless paired with filtration and treatment — the natural attach-on product for anyone selling into this market.
insights.locator: The system doesn’t provide drinking water

themes.theme: Building-code mandates as the adoption lever

insights.claim: Roughly 90 percent of homes in the US Virgin Islands have a cistern to collect rainwater, and the territory's building codes require many new developments to include the infrastructure — a direct demonstration that code mandates, not consumer preference, drive island-wide adoption.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Building-code adoption is the single best leading indicator for rainwater-hardware demand; track code changes in Caribbean and coastal jurisdictions as procurement signals.
insights.locator: Roughly 90 percent of homes in the US Virgin Islands

insights.claim: Honolulu County offers a limited number of free rain barrel installations to residents, showing that US jurisdictions already use direct subsidy rather than mandate alone to seed decentralized water capture.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Subsidy programs create lumpy municipal purchase orders for barrel and cistern manufacturers — a bid pipeline distinct from retail demand.

insights.claim: Puerto Rico's government offers no incentives or financial assistance for rainwater harvesting and does not require catchment systems, unlike some other island states, leaving small nonprofits to meet demand at tiny scale.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Zero policy support means the market is currently philanthropic, not commercial — the upside case requires a policy catalyst, so watch legislative action as the entry trigger.
insights.locator: Yet in Puerto Rico, the government offers no incentives

insights.claim: Farah Nibbs of the University of Maryland Baltimore County argues rainwater harvesting should be treated as part of the national water supply and that governments should cover costs to avoid pushing economic burdens onto households.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Reclassifying decentralized capture as national supply infrastructure is what unlocks public funding streams — the framing to watch in Caribbean water policy.
insights.quote: There is nothing that can help the Caribbean region as quickly and as reliably as rainwater harvesting
insights.locator: There is nothing that can help the Caribbean region

insights.claim: A 2024 Puerto Rico law mandating all public agencies to install rainwater collection systems on government buildings is not being followed by agencies nor enforced, showing that mandate passage without an enforcement mechanism produces no procurement.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Legislated demand that never converts to orders is a common trap in emerging climate-adaptation markets; discount headline mandates until enforcement or budget lines appear.
insights.locator: He points to a 2024 law that mandated all public agencies

insights.claim: At-large legislator José Pérez Cordero introduced a June resolution ordering the Puerto Rican Natural Resources Committee to study rainwater harvesting feasibility based on other Caribbean models, and it has gone nowhere despite mounting water insecurity even though his New Progressive Party holds power.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Even majority-party sponsorship is failing to move adaptation policy in an active crisis — a caution on timing any Puerto Rico climate-infrastructure thesis to political catalysts.
insights.quote: We are, right now, in the perfect moment to do it, because we are in the middle of a crisis
insights.locator: José Pérez Cordero, an at-large legislator

insights.claim: Since 2010 the nonprofit Plenitud Puerto Rico has donated and installed only 73 rainwater harvesting systems in Las Marías, a scale that underscores how far philanthropic delivery falls short of island-wide need.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: 73 units over 15 years versus a 1-million-household opportunity quantifies the gap that only policy or commercial capital can close.
insights.locator: Since 2010, local environmental nonprofit Plenitud Puerto Rico

insights.claim: Rainwater harvesting cannot solve Puerto Rico's water problems in urban locations where large apartment complexes are hard to retrofit, and the systems become unsustainable if the wet season is not rainy enough — a risk rising with fossil-fuel-driven warming.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: The adaptation market is bounded by building typology and precipitation variance; single-family low-rise markets are the realistic beachhead, not dense urban ones.
insights.locator: Rainwater harvesting won’t solve all of Puerto Rico’s water problems

insights.claim: Puerto Rico's July was the driest month on record, driving a historic drought that pushed the territory into water rationing despite annual precipitation ranging from 30 to 169 inches across the island.
insights.speaker: Yessenia Funes
insights.so_what: Record precipitation volatility on a rain-abundant island is the core adaptation thesis: storage buffers, not more supply, are the product the climate is demanding.
insights.locator: Puerto Rico is experiencing a historic drought
